children: 1849 ET - Japanese stocks may rise as fears about an escalation in the Middle East conflict ease. Oil prices fell sharply overnight after President Trump downplayed the prospect of further U.S. strikes on Iran. Nikkei futures are up 3.5% at 60880 on the SGX. The dollar is at 157.99 yen, compared with Y158.26 as of Monday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on domestic earnings and crude oil prices. The Nikkei Stock Average rose 2.3% to 58775.50 on Monday. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com)

1430 ET - Investors show lukewarm demand for three-year Treasury notes in a $58 billion auction. The bid-to-cover ratio comes at 2.53, below the six-month average of 2.64. The Treasury ends up paying 4.627% yield, which is lower than the 4.9% it paid last month, but higher than the when-issued yield of 4.622% at the time of auction. Indirect bidders, the group that includes foreign buyers, took $32 billion of the securities, or 55% of the total sold. That was also below the 63% 12-month average. The three-year yield trades at 4.634%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1404 ET - The dollar weakens as the political backlash against AI infrastructure weighs on the currency. The S&P 500 Information Technology index falls 2%, even as the overall index raises 2%. "We think the US dollar would fall further against most major currencies if AI-related equities' recent troubles continued," Capital Economics' Thomas Mathews writes. The WSJ Dollar Index slips 0.4%, as the greenback weakens 0.6% against the euro and 0.2% versus the yen. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1306 ET - The Federal Reserve's decision making isn't going to be affected by the Democrats sweeping the midterm elections, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says during a Q&A at a Chicago event. That's part of the central bank's mandate to be independent, he says, comparing the Fed with the Night's Watch from Game of Thrones. "You're out of the elections business," he says. The outcome of the election can impact fiscal policy, not the monetary policy handled by the Fed, Goolsbee says. Central bankers will focus on their jobs of balancing prices and employment, and will adapt to the conditions that result from fiscal policy changes, regardless of which party makes them, he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1234 ET - The massive data center buildout spree poses some overheating risks to the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says in a Q&A at a Chicago event. He compares the recent AI boom to the dot-com bubble around 2000, and warns that lofty growth expectations can lead to disappointment. While he doesn't want to call AI a bubble, he notes that there has been an almost unprecedented level of investment in AI. "In the Fed world, the bigger the hype, the more nervous I am that we're going to overheat what the economy is capable of in the next six months," Goolsbee says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1202 ET - Readings of consumer sentiment are broadly important, just not directly applicable to the Federal Reserve's job, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says during a Q&A at a Chicago event. Consumer sentiment has long been a leading indicator for consumer spending, but those two data sets have broken away from each other in the past five years, he says. "Consumer sentiment has been in the toilet for now a long time," while consumer spending has been the main driver of economic growth, Goolsbee says. That makes consumer sentiment less critical for central bankers as they weigh the direction of the economy while deciding on the path of interest rates, he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1152 ET - Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says inflation is the big problem facing the central bank while employment and economic growth are looking stable. Employment is stable without being good, he says, given that the hiring rate is low, but "we've been moving up to what historically we would consider full employment, Goolsbee says during a Q&A at an event in Chicago. "The big problem has all been on the inflation side," he says. Goolsbee is set to return to the Fed's rate-setting committee as a voting member in January. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1057 ET - The eurozone's Sentix indicator, a gauge of investor confidence, fell in November, pointing to subdued growth in the fourth quarter, Oxford Economics' Iain Simmons says in a note. Expectations weakened for a second straight month, while current conditions were unchanged. "The release adds to signals that this summer's upswing in surveys has lost some of its steam, consistent with the moderation in October's PMIs and ESI," Simmons says. Still, the fall was modest, pointing to subdued rather than deteriorating confidence, he adds. Data for Germany was a bright spot as the industrial recovery gains traction, but weaker global sentiment, rising energy costs and higher interest rates threaten to weigh on the eurozone outlook. "Overall, we continue to expect modest Eurozone growth of 0.1% quarter-over-quarter in 4Q." (don.forbes@wsj.com)

1002 ET - The Polish zloty will likely remain under pressure in the coming months, potentially underperforming its regional peers including the Hungarian forint and Czech koruna, Commerzbank's Tatha Ghose says in a note. Ratings agency S&P downgraded its sovereign credit outlook on Poland to negative on Friday due to concerns over the country's deteriorating fiscal outlook amid a political gridlock between pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and nationalist President Karol Nawrocki. Foreign exchange markets have been slow to price in the structural risk premium associated with Poland's political escalation, Ghose says. "Poland's political situation has become a major impediment to economic policymaking." The euro falls 0.1% to 4.3856 zloty after hitting a three-year high of 4.4259 last week, LSEG data show. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0954 ET - The renewal of the Bank of Canada's inflation-targeting framework marks a back-to-basics approach, says economists at National Bank of Canada, citing the removal of references maximum sustainable employment, climate change and income inequality that were introduced in 2021 under the watch of the Justin Trudeau administration. The renewed framework reinforces that price stability, with inflation at 2%, is paramount, NBC says. The statement announcing the renewal makes references to the impact on inflation from global shocks, indicating policymakers "will place greater emphasis on how external shocks pass through to domestic prices." The statement also had no references to core CPI, and NBC wonders whether Gov. Tiff Macklem will reveal in a Nov. 24 speech a new way in which BOC officials will gauge underlying inflation. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

0945 ET - Canada's AAA credit rating remains intact, supported by declining deficits, stable debt-to-GDP and a resilient economy, Morningstar DBRS says. The federal 2026 budget highlighted a government strategy focused and speeding up investment, productivity and long-term economic growth while maintaining fiscal sustainability, Morningstar's Travis Shaw says. He adds that while the government is significantly increasing spending, the budget keeps key fiscal anchors intact, supported by stronger-than-expected revenue driven by a resilient economy and higher energy prices. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0945 ET - Yields on 30-year U.K. government bond fall to the lowest level since July as oil prices extend declines. Lower oil prices are easing inflation fears and reducing the prospects of the Bank of England raising interest rates sharply. Thirty-year gilt yields last trade at 5.558%, having hit a four-month low of 5.538% earlier in the session, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)
